preamble: The diphthong /oi/ was monophthongized to the close front rounded vowel /y/ in post-classical Greek. The change appears first in Boeotian, where 3rd-century BC inscriptions write υ for οι, and was complete in popular Koine by the 1st century BC, when οι and υ merged; both later became /i/. Some scholars posit an intermediate [øː], inferred from Boeotian ει spellings and from the late confusion of οι with υ in Egyptian papyri, but no spelling directly attests it. Outside Greek a direct oi > y change is not documented; related changes more often give [ø] (Nagoya Japanese) or [u] (Latin oi > ū).

examples.note: Egyptian Greek writes υ for οι and confuses the two from the early 1st century BC, showing that οι had merged with υ /y/; both later became /i/.

examples.to: Koine [pyˈe̝sas], spelled πυήσας in a papyrus letter of 100 AD
Koine [my], spelled μυ in the same letter

examples.from: ἄλλοις προξένοις 'to the other proxenoi' (Attic spelling)
examples.note: Boeotian inscriptions from the 3rd century BC write υ for οι, so the monophthongization to [yː] came early in this dialect.

sources: Allen, W. S. (1987). Vox Graeca: A Guide to the Pronunciation of Classical Greek (3rd ed.). Cambridge University Press. https://ci.nii.ac.jp/ncid/BA0124031X
